answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Top-level resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (Cosmos DB accounts).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core Azure CLI group az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=eastus. This is part of the core az CLI (no separate extension required for basic account management).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource of type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Example (Bicep): resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' properties: { databaseAccountOfferType: 'Standard' locations: [ { locationName: 'eastus' } ] kind: 'MongoDB' } }. Terraform (AzureRM): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (set kind = "MongoDB"); optionally use azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database for databases and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection for collections.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical MongoDB-compatible Cosmos DB connection string: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@<account>@. Example: mongodb://myUser:myPassword@sampledb.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed as Cosmos DB throughput (Request Units per second, RUs). You can provision fixed RUs, use autoscale RUs, or (where supported) serverless mode. The MongoDB API on Cosmos DB does not use vCore billing; it uses RU-based throughput.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Data-plane access for the MongoDB wire protocol is typically via MongoDB credentials (username/password / SCRAM auth) created for the account (the standard MongoDB user/password the account exposes). Management plane operations use Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) tokens via the azure CLI/SDK. Native MongoDB drivers authenticate with SCRAM (username/password). Azure AD authentication for the MongoDB wire protocol is not the usual data-plane path; if Azure AD is supported for data-plane it requires special configuration and driver support. For code, you normally supply the Mongo connection string with username/password stored in a secret or environment variable.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For application data access use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo or motor for Python). For async ODM in Python use Beanie (which runs on Motor). There is not a separate data-plane Cosmos-specific MongoDB client; management/ARM operations use azure-mgmt-cosmosdb / azure-identity for control plane.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Vector index support is provider-specific; for a MongoDB-compatible DocumentDB cluster that exposes vector indexes you create an index on the embedding field using createIndex with engine-specific options. Example (committed form I would act on): db.complaints.createIndex( { embedding: 1 }, { name: 'emb_hnsw', background: true, algorithm: 'HNSW', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } ). (Note: keys like algorithm/dims are engine extensions and must match the cluster's vector-index syntax.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Use MongoDB text indexes for basic full-text search (db.coll.createIndex({ field: 'text' })). For richer hybrid (semantic + vector) search, combine the cluster's vector index on embeddings with text search or integrate Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) — e.g., use Cognitive Search for semantic ranking and/or as a pipeline that enriches and indexes documents, while using the MongoDB vector index for similarity filtering.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API supports particular MongoDB wire protocol versions depending on the account's configured API version (historically 3.2/3.6/4.0/4.2/5.0 and more recently 6/7 previews). Expect to choose a MongoDB server version on account creation. Some MongoDB features are limited or different (server-side JavaScript/eval, some advanced aggregation stages or operators, certain transaction semantics, and some admin commands may not be supported). Test critical features against the target account version.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for local development (Microsoft's emulator image mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator). For MongoDB-protocol compatibility you can point drivers at the emulator's Mongo endpoint (commonly port 10255 for TLS). Alternatively, use a real MongoDB server (official mongo Docker image) for pure MongoDB behaviour, but that will not match Cosmos DB engine extensions.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB provides a Change Feed (SQL API) and the MongoDB API exposes change-stream–style functionality depending on the MongoDB wire version supported by the account. In many accounts $changeStream is available for supported API versions; no separate portal toggle is usually required but you must use an account API version that advertises change stream support. For SQL API use the Change Feed APIs/processor which are separate.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (profile name 'documentdb') for data-plane inspection tools for Cosmos DB / DocumentDB. The general Azure MCP server covers many Azure services, but the documentdb MCP server has service-specific tools and inspectors for collections, indexes and query plans.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally branded the service as DocumentDB. It evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (a multi-model, globally distributed DB). The open-source 'DocumentDB' project is unrelated; 'DocumentDB' was Microsoft's original product name before rebranding to Cosmos DB which now offers multiple APIs including SQL (DocumentDB), Gremlin, Table, Cassandra and the MongoDB-compatible API.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Under the MongoDB API the backing engine is Cosmos DB's own storage/engine that implements the MongoDB wire protocol. For most CRUD and basic aggregation queries, MongoDB drivers work unchanged. However, some server features, operators or behaviours differ (indexing/consistency/transactions/aggregation edge-cases), so test and adjust queries and indexes for the Cosmos DB implementation.

answers.question: What exact connection string and environment variable should the sample use to reach the cluster?
answers.answer: Read DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment. Expect a Mongo-style URI on TLS and port 10255, e.g. mongodb://<user>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false. In Python use motor.motor_asyncio.AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']) or pymongo.MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']).

answers.question: Which database and collection names will the sample create and operate on?
answers.answer: Use database name sample_banking_14. Create/operate on at least two collections: complaints (raw and enriched complaint documents) and complaint_embeddings (or complaints with an embedding field). Example creation: db = client['sample_banking_14']; db.create_collection('complaints') if missing.

answers.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search?
answers.answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field with HNSW parameters. Example createIndex I will run: db.complaints.createIndex( { embedding: 1 }, { name: 'emb_hnsw', algorithm: 'HNSW', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine', m: 16, efConstruction: 200, background: true } ). (This uses provider-specific index options; if the cluster requires different names/keys use the MCP inspection tools to adapt.)

answers.question: What aggregation pipeline will surface complaint hotspots by category?
answers.answer: Aggregation pipeline I will use: [ { $match: { category: { $exists: true } } }, { $group: { _id: '$category', count: { $sum: 1 }, topComplaints: { $push: { id: '$_id', text: '$text', urgency: '$urgency' } } } }, { $sort: { count: -1 } }, { $project: { category: '$_id', count: 1, topComplaints: { $slice: ['$topComplaints', 5] } } } ]. Run with db.complaints.aggregate(pipeline).

answers.question: How will the app authenticate and initialize Beanie ODM in Python?
answers.answer: Use Motor with the MongoDB connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass the Motor client to Beanie. Example code I would run: from motor.motor_asyncio import AsyncIOMotorClient; client = AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']); from beanie import init_beanie; await init_beanie(database=client['sample_banking_14'], document_models=[Complaint]);
